pillar_reactions.evidence: Delivered first and correctly prioritised to what the prospect had just named — 'for you, probably the mobility is going to be the main thing that we're going to start from because that's the foundation for all the movements' — with a decent tie to his sport: 'whenever an idea pops up to your head, hey, let's do a high rocks tomorrow in some distance, you're going to be ready.' The response was a flat 'Yeah' and, at the check, 'Makes sense? Yeah.' Accepted rather than enthusiastic: no elaboration, no question, nothing volunteered. The tailoring promise stayed generic ('any stiffness that you have, could have, and potentially like in hips, shoulders, whatever') and never named the two things the rep had just spent five minutes uncovering — four labral tears held together by stem cell injections and a rodded right leg with eight screws. Specific would have landed; generic did not.

Pre-conceded as in every other call in this batch — 'It sounds like you have dialed in' — then the standard three variables with the weekly free day. One genuinely responsive touch: the rep tied it back to the travel problem he had surfaced, 'with a plan that he will prepare you, it will be probably easier for you to sustain it when you're traveling. Of course, you can have a dessert.' That is the pillar doing its job against a disclosed pain, and the prospect had just admitted 'one bite turns into 20' on the road. It still drew only 'Okay.' No questions, no pushback, no engagement — accepted. Worth noting the rapport detour immediately before it, where the rep spent about a minute on an Alex Hormozi 'never skip dessert' reference that the prospect did not recognise and that produced nothing.

The decisive row in this file. The rep opened the pillar by inviting the prospect to reject it: 'And the third part, you said that you don't need hand-holding. Is that correct?' The prospect obliged — 'No, I mean, like, I'm sure a lot of other clients, like, you got to get them to actually work out every day. I'm going to be doing that, so.' The rep then delivered the pillar anyway (direct number, over-communication, video form review, weekly check-ins, roughly a month to learn the movements) against a prospect who had just been handed permission to dismiss it. He objected in substance twice more once price was on the table: 'after month one, like you mentioned, like, I don't really need, I don't see myself needing the additional check-ins', and 'I'd rather just pay for a program is really where my head's at, more so than paying for an ongoing handholding.' He had actually pre-flagged it in discovery too, at 00:07:55 — 'for me, it's probably less of a one-on-one coaching... and more so, like, just getting a program, working on it, like, using you guys as a resource when I need to.' The objection was visible eight minutes before the pillar was delivered and the pillar was framed to concede it rather than to answer it.

anchors.raw: I spend, you know, 1,500, 2K a month sometimes on trainers when I'm here, not traveling as much. And it's like, I could probably, you know, I don't know, to spend the same amount for virtual seems a little crazy.
anchors.competitor: In-person personal trainers in Los Angeles, $1,500-$2,000 per month
anchors.note: The most double-edged anchor in the corpus and the rep used neither edge. As deployed by the prospect it undercuts: he treats in-person as the premium format and remote as the discount one, so $6,000 for six months of virtual reads as overpriced against $1,500-$2,000 a month of in-person. But the same sentence is the strongest affordability proof anywhere in this batch — he is spending $18,000 to $24,000 a year on coaching, which makes $6,000 for six months roughly half his current run rate for a service he can use in Mykonos. Nobody did that arithmetic out loud.

anchors.raw: Like, it's not even like the $4,000. I spend way more on stupid [stuff] all the time.
anchors.note: A prospect ruling out his own price objection, unprompted. This is the line that should have redirected the entire close: the constraint is scope, not cost, and every subsequent discount was therefore solving a problem that did not exist. Logged prominently because it is the counter-example to the rest of the batch — this is the one prospect in the set for whom $6,000 was genuinely affordable, and he is also the one who was discounted to $1,500.

anchors.raw: But it's just, for what I want, and all the online resources and things, like, it just seems silly for me to spend so much money on. In my mind, what I want is just a program.
anchors.note: Third appearance of the free-content anchor across four sales calls in this batch. Weaker here than in the Jorge Fernández call — he is not actually using free resources and named them almost in passing — but it went entirely unanswered, and its recurrence rate is now the finding rather than any single instance.

anchors.raw: I ended up getting stem cells instead of surgery.
anchors.note: Pattern of buying the expensive option in health: elective stem cell therapy over surgery for four labral tears, a boutique circuit-gym membership stacked on top of a regular gym, Hyrox race entry with a 15-hour flight to Barcelona, and a travel pattern spanning Mykonos, Ibiza, Saint-Tropez and Marbella. Nothing about this prospect is price-sensitive, and none of it was reflected back when the number was named.

anchors.raw: Three months is 4K... Would you be down for, like, 30 days just checking how it works?... Yeah, so for three months, that would be 1,500.
anchors.note: The only anchor in the corpus created by Primal rather than by the prospect, and it is the most damaging one on this call. Inside four minutes the number went $6,000, then $4,000, then $1,500, each step triggered by hesitation rather than by any new information. The prospect learned, correctly, that hesitating lowers the price — and then hesitated again, at which point the rep booked a follow-up rather than closing. Whatever the merits of a trial product, teaching a wealthy prospect that the price is negotiable in real time destroys the premium positioning that justifies $6,000 in the first place.

unmet_demand.want: A programming-only product — the workouts and progressions without the ongoing coaching relationship. Stated three times and finally in plain words: 'what I want is not necessarily something that you guys normally sell. Like, I just want to buy a program.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The offer is one-to-one coaching with Trevor by definition, and all three pillars assume the relationship. There is no program-only tier at any price, and the rep's response to the request was to shorten the coaching rather than to unbundle it. This is the cleanest product gap in the batch because the prospect named the missing SKU himself, could afford it, and was ready to buy it.

unmet_demand.want: A short, low-commitment way to test the product before buying the full engagement — 'if there's a 30-day hybrid, I'd be open to that for sure.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The rep invented one on the call, at $1,500 for 30 days, branded 'love it or leave it', with no refund mechanics, no written terms and no evidence of authorisation. The internal onboarding call recorded the previous day establishes that non-standard structures are 'not generally an option that we offer'. So the want was met by something that may not exist. Flagged for a human: either a 30-day trial is a real product and should be priced and documented, or a prospect has been quoted one that cannot be honoured.

unmet_demand.want: Conditioning that complements Hyrox racing — he competes recreationally, intends to do more, and trains twice a day already.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The rep touched it once in passing ('let's do a high rocks tomorrow... you're going to be ready') and never addressed the actual question, which is how kettlebell work slots alongside an existing twice-daily programme without simply adding volume to a man with four repaired labra. Whether the programme is designed to replace, supplement or conflict with his current training was never established, and that ambiguity is part of why he could only see it as 'a program' rather than a system.

unmet_demand.want: Loading that respects two stem-cell-treated shoulders with four labral tears and a right leg containing a metal bar and eight screws.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The rep drew the injuries out well and then never mentioned them again. The training and mobility pillar promised generic attention to 'any stiffness that you have, could have', with no reference to the specific structures involved and no question about clearance or load limits — despite the prospect volunteering that pain returns 'when I'm doing like a ton of volume and a ton of reps', which is a direct constraint on how a kettlebell programme should be written for him. Same clinical blind spot recorded across this batch.
